Threads, SIMD, task parallelism, and performance analysis.

Program Contents P1 · CPU threads Worker code, row assignment, load balance, and scaling P2 · SIMD intrinsics Vector code, masks, and lane utilization P3 · ISPC SIMD execution, task count, and speedup P4 · Iterative sqrt Input-dependent convergence and divergence P5 · SAXPY Memory bandwidth and cache traffic P6 · K-means Profiling, worker code, debugging, and verification

Required work completed. Extra credit: P2's array sum and P4's AVX2 implementation are complete; P5's optimization was skipped.

Measurement method · Handout

docs.title: Timing method
docs.text:
Unless noted otherwise, results use default CPU scheduling.

  • P1 and P3–P5: median of three program runs. Each run reports its best internal repetition: five in P1, three in P3–P5. P1's total includes worker printing.
  • P6: median of three complete algorithm runs, excluding data loading. Phase timings come from separate profiling runs.

P5 uses single-core ISPC as its baseline; the other timed programs use serial code.

docs.title: P1 · Mandelbrot with threads
docs.text:
Render a 1600 × 1200 image with std::thread, using at most 256 iterations per pixel.

Views 1 and 2 from the handout. Brighter pixels require more computation.

docs.title: 1. Split the image between two threads
docs.text:
workerThreadStart in mandelbrotThread.cpp:

void workerThreadStart(WorkerArgs * const args) {
    int startRow = 0;
    int numRows = args->height / 2;

    if (args->threadId == 1) {
        startRow = args->height / 2;
    }

    mandelbrotSerial(args->x0, args->y0, args->x1, args->y1,
                     args->width, args->height,
                     startRow, numRows,
                     args->maxIterations,
                     args->output);
}

docs.title: 1.1 How the row range controls the work
docs.text:
startRow and numRows select the rows to render. Thread 0 handles [0, 600) and thread 1 handles [600, 1200).

The complex-plane bounds (x0, y0, x1, y1) and full image dimensions stay unchanged, preserving the pixel coordinates in both workers.

Pixel (r, c) is stored at output[r * width + c]. The workers share the output array but write disjoint rows, so no lock is needed.

docs.title: 1.2 Where the second thread comes from
docs.text: The starter's mandelbrotThread launches worker 1 with std::thread, runs worker 0 on the calling thread, and joins worker 1 before returning.

docs.title: 2. Extend to 2–8 threads
docs.text:
void workerThreadStart(WorkerArgs * const args) {
    int numRows = args->height / args->numThreads;
    int startRow = args->threadId * numRows;

    if (args->threadId == args->numThreads - 1) {
        numRows = args->height - startRow;
    }

    mandelbrotSerial(args->x0, args->y0, args->x1, args->y1,
                     args->width, args->height,
                     startRow, numRows,
                     args->maxIterations,
                     args->output);
}

docs.title: 2.1 Block assignment
docs.text:
Let q = height / numThreads, using integer division. Worker t starts at t * q and initially receives q rows.

With seven threads, equal blocks cover only 7 × 171 = 1197 rows. The last worker starts at row 1026 and takes 1200 - 1026 = 174 rows, including the three-row remainder. This fixes the seven-thread mismatch.

docs.title: 2.2 Scaling results
docs.text:
The contiguous-block version gives the following speedups:

Scaling is not linear. For view 1, speedup falls from 1.98× with two threads to 1.61× with three. Pixels require different numbers of iterations, so equally sized blocks can contain very different amounts of work. The middle block is the likely bottleneck.

docs.title: 3. Measure each worker
docs.text:
Add a timer around the block computation:

void workerThreadStart(WorkerArgs * const args) {
    double startTime = CycleTimer::currentSeconds();

    int numRows = args->height / args->numThreads;
    int startRow = args->threadId * numRows;

    if (args->threadId == args->numThreads - 1) {
        numRows = args->height - startRow;
    }

    mandelbrotSerial(args->x0, args->y0, args->x1, args->y1,
                     args->width, args->height,
                     startRow, numRows,
                     args->maxIterations,
                     args->output);

    double endTime = CycleTimer::currentSeconds();
    printf("Thread %d: %.3f ms\n",
           args->threadId, (endTime-startTime)*1000);
}

For view 1 with three threads, median worker times over 15 invocations were:

Worker Time (ms) 0 49.825 1 151.085 2 51.046

The middle block takes roughly three times as long as the outer blocks. Rendering must wait for this slowest worker, confirming that load imbalance causes the poor three-thread result.

docs.title: 4. Interleave the rows
docs.text:
void workerThreadStart(WorkerArgs * const args) {
    double startTime = CycleTimer::currentSeconds();

    for (unsigned int i = args->threadId;
         i < args->height;
         i += args->numThreads) {
        mandelbrotSerial(args->x0, args->y0, args->x1, args->y1,
                         args->width, args->height,
                         i, 1,
                         args->maxIterations,
                         args->output);
    }

    double endTime = CycleTimer::currentSeconds();
    printf("Thread %d: %.3f ms\n",
           args->threadId, (endTime-startTime)*1000);
}

docs.title: 4.1 Row assignment
docs.text:
Worker t starts at row t and advances by numThreads. Each call with arguments i, 1 renders one row:

12 rows, 3 workers; entries are row numbers

              Contiguous blocks       Interleaved rows
              +-------------+         +-------------+
Worker 0      |  0  1  2  3 |         |  0  3  6  9 |
Worker 1      |  4  5  6  7 |         |  1  4  7 10 |
Worker 2      |  8  9 10 11 |         |  2  5  8 11 |
              +-------------+         +-------------+

Each row r belongs to worker r % numThreads, giving every row exactly one owner. The loop condition handles the bottom of the image even when the height is not divisible by the thread count.

Spreading rows throughout the image gives every worker a mixture of cheap and expensive pixels. In view 1, the costly middle region is shared across workers. This static mapping needs no communication during rendering and applies to both views.

docs.title: 4.2 Results
docs.text:
The three worker times for view 1 become 84.584, 88.906, and 88.950 ms, much closer together.

Final eight-thread results:

View Serial (ms) 8 threads (ms) Speedup 1 241.408 41.502 5.82× 2 135.515 24.461 5.54×

Both views pass the pixel-by-pixel serial comparison.

docs.title: 4.3 Comparison with the handout
docs.text:
The handout expects about 7–8× with eight threads.

The local i9-13900H combines six P cores and eight E cores, unlike the handout's four-core i7-7700K. Static row assignment gives each worker a similar amount of work, while completion time depends on the slowest worker's throughput. Core placement and clock behavior also affect the serial baseline.

A separate comparison tested default scheduling against restricting both serial and parallel runs to the eight E cores:

View CPU selection Serial (ms) 8 threads (ms) Speedup 1 Default 343.321 58.922 5.83× 1 Eight E cores 530.944 66.802 7.95× 2 Default 192.635 34.322 5.61× 2 Eight E cores 316.804 40.039 7.91×

The E-core results approach 8× partly because their serial baseline is slower. Default scheduling still gives shorter parallel runtimes.

docs.title: 5. Compare 8 and 16 threads
docs.text:
Using the improved, interleaved version:

View 8 threads (ms) 16 threads (ms) 16-thread speedup over serial Gain over 8 threads 1 41.502 23.285 10.36× 1.78× 2 24.461 14.049 9.65× 1.74×

Sixteen threads improve performance on this machine. It has 14 physical cores and 20 logical CPUs, so additional threads can use more execution resources.

Measurement method

docs.title: P2 · Masked exponentiation
docs.text: Compute values[i]^exponents[i] and clamp each result to 9.999999f with the course's simulated SIMD intrinsics.

docs.title: 1. Vectorize clamped exponentiation
docs.text:
clampedExpVector in main.cpp:

void clampedExpVector(float* values, int* exponents,
                      float* output, int N) {
    __cs149_vec_float x;
    __cs149_vec_int y;
    __cs149_vec_float result;
    __cs149_vec_int zero = _cs149_vset_int(0);
    __cs149_vec_int one = _cs149_vset_int(1);
    __cs149_vec_float ninef = _cs149_vset_float(9.999999f);
    __cs149_vec_int count;
    __cs149_mask maskEff, maskIsEqual, maskIsNotEqual;

    for (int i=0; i<N; i+=VECTOR_WIDTH) {
        maskEff = _cs149_init_ones(N-i);
        maskIsEqual = _cs149_init_ones(0);
        _cs149_vload_float(x, values+i, maskEff);
        _cs149_vload_int(y, exponents+i, maskEff);
        _cs149_veq_int(maskIsEqual, y, zero, maskEff);

        _cs149_vset_float(result, 1.f, maskIsEqual);

        maskIsNotEqual = _cs149_mask_not(maskIsEqual);
        maskIsNotEqual = _cs149_mask_and(maskIsNotEqual, maskEff);
        _cs149_vsub_int(count, y, one, maskIsNotEqual);
        _cs149_vmove_float(result, x, maskIsNotEqual);
        _cs149_vgt_int(maskIsNotEqual, count, zero, maskIsNotEqual);

        while (_cs149_cntbits(maskIsNotEqual)) {
            _cs149_vmult_float(result, result, x, maskIsNotEqual);
            _cs149_vsub_int(count, count, one, maskIsNotEqual);
            _cs149_vgt_int(maskIsNotEqual, count, zero, maskIsNotEqual);
        }

        _cs149_vgt_float(maskIsNotEqual, result, ninef, maskEff);
        _cs149_vset_float(result, 9.999999f, maskIsNotEqual);
        _cs149_vstore_float(output+i, result, maskEff);
    }
}

docs.title: 1.1 Load a vector and mark valid lanes
docs.text:
Within a batch starting at i, lane j holds array element i + j. A zero mask bit preserves that lane's previous destination value.

maskEff = _cs149_init_ones(N-i) enables the first min(VECTOR_WIDTH, N-i) lanes. Loads and stores use this mask to keep the final partial vector within the array.

docs.title: 1.2 Translate the exponent cases into masks
docs.text:
maskIsEqual starts with all lanes disabled, then _cs149_veq_int enables valid lanes whose exponent is zero. Those lanes receive result = 1 and need no multiplication.

The other valid lanes are selected by ~maskIsEqual & maskEff. The AND is necessary because inverting a mask also turns on the unused lanes in a partial vector:

N = 6, width = 4, i = 4; lane 0 is on the left

Array index                 4  5  -  -
Example exponent            0  3  -  -
maskEff                     1  1  0  0
maskIsEqual                 1  0  0  0
~maskIsEqual                0  1  1  1
~maskIsEqual & maskEff      0  1  0  0

Positive-exponent lanes begin with result = x and count = y - 1, since one factor of x is already present. The first count > 0 test excludes exponent-one lanes from the loop.

docs.title: 1.3 Follow the multiplication loop
docs.text:
maskIsNotEqual tracks lanes with count > 0. Only active lanes multiply and decrement; each comparison drops finished lanes. _cs149_cntbits keeps the loop running while any lane is active.

For bases [2, 2, 2, 2] and exponents [0, 1, 3, 5]:

Stage          Mask used     Result after this stage   Remaining count
Initialize         -         1   2   2   2             -  0  2  4
Multiply 1       0 0 1 1      1   2   4   4             -  0  1  3
Multiply 2       0 0 1 1      1   2   8   8             -  0  0  2
Multiply 3       0 0 0 1      1   2   8  16             -  0  0  1
Multiply 4       0 0 0 1      1   2   8  32             -  0  0  0
Exit             0 0 0 0

Finished results are preserved while the longest-running lane keeps the loop active.

docs.title: 1.4 Clamp and store
docs.text: The final comparison uses maskEff to rebuild the mask for result > 9.999999f. After clamping, the example becomes [1, 2, 8, 9.999999]. The store uses maskEff to write all valid results, including exponent-zero and unclamped lanes.

docs.title: 1.5 Debugging and verification
docs.text:
The absVector warm-up exposed the tail-mask issue: inverting a predicate re-enabled invalid lanes. Intersecting the complement with maskEff fixed the N = 3, W = 4 case.

The first exponentiation loop used maskIsEqual for multiplication while testing maskIsNotEqual for continuation. Using the active mask consistently, testing count > 0 before entry, and adding the clamp fixed the failures.

The required function passes at widths 2, 4, 8, and 16, including partial vectors. At width 4, the original tests covered N = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 16, 10000.

docs.title: 2. Compare vector utilization
docs.text:
For N = 10,000:

Width Vector instructions Utilization 2 167,727 77.6% 4 97,075 70.5% 8 52,877 66.7% 16 27,592 65.0%

A wider vector is more likely to contain a long-running lane. Finished lanes remain inactive while that lane continues, reducing utilization. More elements are processed per instruction, so total instruction count still falls.

docs.title: 3. Extra credit: array sum
docs.text: Assume N is a multiple of VECTOR_WIDTH.

docs.title: 3.1 Accumulate and reduce
docs.text:
float arraySumVector(float* values, int N) {
    __cs149_vec_float x;
    __cs149_vec_float result;
    // The simulator's interleave needs distinct source and destination vectors.
    __cs149_vec_float temp;
    __cs149_mask maskAll, maskEff, maskNotEff;
    float ans = 0.f;

    maskAll = _cs149_init_ones();
    maskEff = _cs149_init_ones(VECTOR_WIDTH/2);
    maskNotEff = _cs149_mask_not(maskEff);

    _cs149_vload_float(x, values, maskAll);
    _cs149_hadd_float(temp, x);
    _cs149_interleave_float(x, temp);
    _cs149_vmove_float(result, x, maskEff);

    for (int i=VECTOR_WIDTH; i<N; i+=VECTOR_WIDTH) {
        _cs149_vload_float(x, values+i, maskAll);
        _cs149_hadd_float(temp, x);
        _cs149_interleave_float(x, temp);
        _cs149_vmove_float(result, x, maskNotEff);
        _cs149_hadd_float(temp, result);
        _cs149_interleave_float(result, temp);
    }
    for (int i=0; i<VECTOR_WIDTH/2; i++) {
        ans += result.value[i];
    }

    return ans;
}

The lower half of result holds partial sums; the upper half receives the next chunk's pair sums. hadd combines adjacent lanes, and interleave packs the unique sums back into the lower half. The final scalar loop adds those lanes. For width W, the work is O(N/W + W).

docs.title: 3.2 Simulator limitation
docs.text:
The original code called interleave(x, x). The interface comments do not mention a restriction on using the same vector for input and output, but the simulator writes destination lanes before reading all source lanes. At width 4, [a, a, b, b] becomes [a, b, b, b] instead of [a, b, a, b]. A single chunk passes because only the intact lower half is used; later chunks read the corrupted upper half.

Writing each hadd result into temp gives interleave distinct input and output vectors. This preserves the original reduction algorithm and adds no vector instructions.

The corrected version passes at widths 2, 4, 8, and 16, covering one chunk, multiple chunks, and N = 10,000.

docs.title: P3 · SIMD and tasks
docs.text: Render a 1200 × 800 Mandelbrot image using SIMD within each core and tasks across cores.

docs.title: Part 1 · Single-core SIMD
docs.text:
The avx2-i32x8 compiler target sets programCount = 8: eight program instances form a gang. foreach distributes pixels among those instances.

Eight-wide SIMD gives an ideal speedup near 8× under the handout's model.

View Serial (ms) ISPC (ms) Speedup 1 121.300 34.424 3.52× 2 68.568 24.183 2.84×

Pixels in a vector can require different iteration counts. Finished lanes are masked off while the slowest lane continues. This is particularly costly near fractal boundaries, where nearby pixels can have very different escape counts. Mask handling and loop control add overhead as well.

docs.title: 2.1 Measure the two-task version
docs.text:
launch creates tasks for the runtime's worker threads. Each task executes as a gang and processes its region in batches of pixels. The original two-task version assigns 400 rows to each task.

For view 1, it takes 18.391 ms: 6.62× over serial and 1.87× over single-core ISPC. Two tasks leave most of the local CPU's cores idle.

docs.title: 2.2 Increase the task count
docs.text:
The implementation uses 200 tasks, each covering four rows. More tasks provide additional parallel work and let workers take another region when they finish.

launch[200]
    |
    v
[task 0] [task 1] ... [task 199]    four rows per task
    |
    | runtime schedules tasks on worker threads
    v
One running task
+-----------------------------------------+
| Gang: [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7]   |  programCount = 8
| foreach -> successive batches of pixels |
+-----------------------------------------+

A task-count sweep gives:

Tasks Rows per task View 1 time (ms) Speedup over serial 2 400 18.391 6.62× 8 100 9.425 12.90× 32 25 3.581 33.85× 200 4 2.752 44.08× 400 2 2.770 43.81× 800 1 2.746 44.24×

View 1 reaches a plateau around 200 tasks. Task size balances load distribution against scheduling overhead.

Results for the current 200-task version:

View Task ISPC (ms) Serial / tasks ISPC / tasks 1 2.752 44.08× 12.51× 2 2.185 31.38× 11.07×

Both ISPC outputs match the serial image. The selected task counts divide all 800 rows evenly.

The handout's 32× target is exceeded on view 1. View 2 improves from 2.185 ms at 200 tasks to 1.970 ms at 800 tasks, giving 34.80×. The smaller tasks improve scheduling on this 20-logical-CPU machine; the useful task count depends on both the machine and the image.

docs.title: 2.3 Extra credit: tasks and threads
docs.text:
A std::thread has an OS-scheduled execution context and its own stack. ISPC tasks share a pool of worker threads. Ten thousand tasks can be queued and processed by that pool; ten thousand OS threads incur much larger creation, memory, and scheduling costs.

join waits for a particular thread. ISPC sync waits for tasks launched by the current function, and function return also synchronizes them. See the ISPC tasking model.

docs.title: 2.4 Why separate foreach and launch?
docs.text: SIMD and multicore scheduling operate at different granularities. Keeping them separate lets a short loop use SIMD with little overhead and a larger workload be divided into tasks. It also lets an application use ISPC inside an existing thread pool. A higher-level parallel-loop construct could combine both mechanisms.

docs.title: P4 · Iterative square root
docs.text:
Compute square roots for 20 million floats with eight-wide SIMD and 64 tasks. Newton iteration starts from a guess of 1; input 1 converges immediately, while 2.999f requires many iterations. All tested inputs pass the supplied 1e-4 absolute-error check.

Iteration count with an initial guess of 1 (handout).

docs.title: 1. Measure SIMD and multicore speedup
docs.text:
With the original random input:

Implementation Time (ms) Speedup over serial Serial 546.799 — ISPC 141.842 3.85× Task ISPC 12.157 44.98×

Multicore execution gives 11.67× speedup over single-core ISPC.

docs.title: 2. Increase relative speedup
docs.text:
Setting every value to 2.999f keeps all lanes active for the same number of iterations. This improves SIMD utilization and amortizes fixed overhead.

Implementation Time (ms) Speedup over serial Serial 1021.521 — ISPC 228.431 4.47× Task ISPC 21.691 47.09×

These are the highest relative speedups among the tested inputs. The additional multicore factor is 10.53×, slightly below the random-input result. Uniform lane workloads benefit both ISPC versions, so their ratio changes much less than the serial-to-SIMD ratio.

docs.title: 3. Decrease relative speedup
docs.text:
Repeat groups of one 2.999f and seven 1.f values. One lane keeps the SIMD loop running while seven lanes are inactive. Serial execution performs the long iteration for only one element in each group.

Input Serial (ms) ISPC (ms) Tasks (ms) Serial / ISPC Serial / tasks One slow, seven fast 146.701 228.311 22.896 0.64× 6.41× All 1.f 10.613 6.486 2.944 1.64× 3.60×

The mixed input leaves ISPC time close to the all-2.999f case while greatly reducing serial work. For all-1 input, a cheap serial baseline reduces speedup, while uniform lane workloads avoid divergence.

docs.title: 4. Extra credit: AVX2 intrinsics
docs.text:
sqrtAVX2 in sqrtAVX2.cpp:

#include <immintrin.h>
#include <climits>

void sqrtAVX2(int N,
                float initialGuess,
                float values[],
                float output[])
{
    static const __m256 kThreshold = _mm256_set1_ps(0.00001f);

    __m256 x;
    __m256 guess1;
    __m256 guess2;
    __m256 guess3;
    __m256 error;

    for (int i=0; i<N; i+=8) {
        x = _mm256_loadu_ps(values+i);
        guess1 = _mm256_set1_ps(initialGuess);

        guess2 = _mm256_mul_ps(guess1, guess1);
        error = _mm256_fmsub_ps(guess2, x, _mm256_set1_ps(1.f));
        error = _mm256_and_ps(error,
            _mm256_castsi256_ps(_mm256_set1_epi32(INT_MAX)));

        while (_mm256_movemask_ps(
            _mm256_cmp_ps(error, kThreshold, _CMP_GT_OQ))) {
            guess3 = _mm256_mul_ps(guess2, guess1);
            guess1 = _mm256_sub_ps(
                _mm256_mul_ps(_mm256_set1_ps(3.f), guess1),
                _mm256_mul_ps(x, guess3));
            guess1 = _mm256_mul_ps(guess1, _mm256_set1_ps(0.5f));
            guess2 = _mm256_mul_ps(guess1, guess1);
            error = _mm256_fmsub_ps(guess2, x, _mm256_set1_ps(1.f));
            error = _mm256_and_ps(error,
                _mm256_castsi256_ps(_mm256_set1_epi32(INT_MAX)));
        }

        _mm256_storeu_ps(output+i, _mm256_mul_ps(x, guess1));
    }
}

docs.title: 4.1 Load eight independent inputs
docs.text: __m256 holds eight 32-bit floats. loadu loads eight consecutive values without requiring alignment; set1 broadcasts the initial guess. The function assumes N is divisible by eight, as it is for the 20-million-element input.

docs.title: 4.2 Update the reciprocal-square-root estimate
docs.text:
For one input x, the iteration solves f(g) = 1/g² - x = 0, so g approaches 1/sqrt(x). Substituting f'(g) = -2/g³ into Newton's update gives:

g_new = g - f(g) / f'(g)
      = (3*g - x*g³) / 2

sqrt(x) = x * (1/sqrt(x)) ≈ x * g

The vector variables follow this calculation lane by lane:

Variable Value in one lane x Input, unchanged during iteration guess1 Current estimate g guess2 g², reused in the error test and next update guess3 g³, formed from guess2 * guess1 error Residual abs(x * g² - 1)

docs.title: 4.3 Compute the absolute residual
docs.text:
_mm256_fmsub_ps evaluates guess2 * x - 1 with fused multiply-subtract, rounding once for the combined operation.

INT_MAX supplies the pattern 0x7fffffff. The cast preserves this bit pattern, and _mm256_and_ps clears each residual's sign bit to obtain its absolute value. The convergence threshold is 1e-5.

docs.title: 4.4 Turn eight comparisons into one loop condition
docs.text:
_mm256_cmp_ps tests error > kThreshold in each lane. With _CMP_GT_OQ, a true comparison produces 0xffffffff and a false comparison produces zero. _mm256_movemask_ps gathers the sign bit of each result into an integer, with lane 0 becoming bit 0. Thus the integer is nonzero whenever any lane still needs work. See the AVX intrinsic definitions.

Lane                         0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
Input                    2.999  1  1  1  1  1  1  1
Needs another iteration?     1  0  0  0  0  0  0  0
                                  |
                                  v
movemask = 00000001 (binary) -> continue
movemask = 00000000 (binary) -> exit

The mask controls the whole while loop; arithmetic still updates all eight lanes. The seven fast lanes stay at g = 1, while the 2.999f lane determines the iteration count.

docs.title: 4.5 Performance
docs.text:
Fresh measurements for 20 million values, with both single-core implementations pinned to the same P core of the local i9-13900H. The C++ build uses GCC 13.3 with -O3 -march=native; ISPC 1.28.1 uses avx2-i32x8.

Input ISPC (ms) AVX2 (ms) ISPC / AVX2 Random 197.448 132.162 1.49× All 2.999f 385.246 153.689 2.51× One slow, seven fast 318.797 153.611 2.08× All 1.f 6.901 6.983 0.99×

All four inputs pass the 1e-4 absolute-error check with finite outputs. The all-2.999f ISPC times range from 318 to 451 ms across the three runs. All-1 input skips the iteration loop, leaving little arithmetic overhead to remove.

docs.title: 4.6 Generated assembly
docs.text:
The AVX2 iteration loop, in Intel syntax. On entry, ymm0 holds guess1, ymm1 holds guess2, and ymm3 holds x:

.L7:
    vmulps        ymm1, ymm0, ymm1       ; guess3 = guess1 * guess2
    vmulps        ymm0, ymm0, ymm8       ; 3 * guess1
    vfnmadd132ps  ymm1, ymm0, ymm3       ; 3 * guess1 - x * guess3
    vmulps        ymm0, ymm1, ymm7       ; new guess1 = above * 0.5
    vmulps        ymm1, ymm0, ymm0       ; guess2 for error and next iteration
    vmovaps       ymm2, ymm1
    vfmsub132ps   ymm2, ymm5, ymm3       ; guess2 * x - 1
    vandps        ymm2, ymm2, ymm4       ; absolute error
    vcmpps        ymm2, ymm2, ymm6, 30   ; error > threshold
    vmovmskps     eax, ymm2
    test          eax, eax
    jne           .L7

The corresponding ISPC loop:

.LBB3_11:
    vmulps       ymm13, ymm9, ymm12      ; x * guess
    vmulps       ymm13, ymm12, ymm13     ; x * guess * guess
    vmulps       ymm13, ymm12, ymm13     ; x * guess * guess * guess
    vfmsub231ps  ymm13, ymm12, ymm7      ; 3 * guess - above
    vmulps       ymm13, ymm13, ymm8      ; new guess
    vblendvps    ymm12, ymm12, ymm13, ymm11 ; update active lanes
    vmulps       ymm13, ymm12, ymm12
    vfmadd213ps  ymm13, ymm9, ymm4       ; guess * guess * x - 1
    vandps       ymm13, ymm13, ymm5      ; absolute error
    vblendvps    ymm10, ymm10, ymm13, ymm11 ; update active lanes
    vcmpltps     ymm13, ymm6, ymm10
    vtestps      ymm13, ymm11
    vandps       ymm11, ymm13, ymm11     ; retain unfinished lanes
    jne          .LBB3_11

The AVX2 loop reuses g² from the error calculation to form g³ directly. ISPC builds x*g, x*g², and x*g³ through three dependent multiplications. Reusing the square shortens this dependency chain.

ISPC uses two vblendvps instructions to preserve finished lanes and a final vandps to maintain the active mask. AVX2 updates every lane and needs only an any-lane test, removing these selection operations while retaining the slowest-lane iteration count.

Both versions use eight-wide arithmetic and FMA. The shorter update chain and simpler lane handling explain the AVX2 improvement on iterative inputs.

Measurements

docs.title: P5 · SAXPY and memory bandwidth
docs.text: SAXPY computes result[i] = scale * X[i] + Y[i] for 20 million floats. The task version uses 64 tasks.

docs.title: 1. Measure and explain task speedup
docs.text:
Implementation Time (ms) Estimated bandwidth (GiB/s) GFLOPS Single-core ISPC 8.266 36.054 4.839 Task ISPC 4.156 71.709 9.625

Both outputs match serial execution. Tasks provide 1.99× speedup.

Each element performs two floating-point operations for an estimated 16 bytes of traffic: 0.125 FLOP/byte. This low arithmetic intensity makes memory bandwidth the expected bottleneck.

Multiple cores keep more memory requests in flight, but share the available bandwidth. Scaling levels off as that bandwidth saturates, so near-linear scaling with core count is not expected for this workload. Further improvement depends on reducing traffic or using the memory system more efficiently.

The driver calculates both rates from elapsed time:

  • GFLOPS = 2N / seconds / 10⁹
  • bandwidth = 16N / seconds / 1024³

The bandwidth estimate uses the traffic model below. Its unit is GiB/s, although the driver prints “GB/s.”

docs.title: 2. Extra credit: explain memory traffic
docs.text:
With write-allocate, write-back caching:

Transfer Bytes per element Read X 4 Read Y 4 Fetch the destination cache line on a store miss 4, amortized Write back the modified destination line 4, amortized Total 16

A store miss fetches the destination line into cache before modifying it. That extra read accounts for the fourth transfer in TOTAL_BYTES = 4 * N * sizeof(float).

docs.title: 1. Prepare the data and measure serial runtime
docs.text: The starter generates 1,000,000 points, 100 dimensions, and 3 clusters. The original serial implementation takes 5813.935 ms (median of three runs).

docs.title: 2. Inspect the clustering
docs.text:
Local data projected to two dimensions by PCA. Colors show assignments; red stars mark centroids.

Handout example (2-D data)

docs.title: 3. Locate the performance bottleneck
docs.text:
Phase times across 24 serial iterations:

Phase Time (ms) Assignment 3751.303 Centroid update 921.564 Cost 1157.595

computeAssignments accounts for 64% of the phase time. Here M is the number of points, N the dimensions per point, and K the number of clusters. Comparing every point with every centroid takes O(M × K × N) work per iteration.

Each point's assignment can be computed independently from the current centroids. With one million points and only three centroids, dividing the points gives many independent units of work and lets each worker finish a complete nearest-centroid search.

docs.title: 4. Parallelize the assignment phase
docs.text:
workerThreadStart in kmeansThread.cpp:

void workerThreadStart(WorkerArgs * const args, double *minDist) {
    for (int m = args->threadId * args->M;
         m < (args->threadId+1) * args->M; m++) {
        for (int k = args->start; k < args->end; k++) {
            double d = dist(&args->data[m * args->N],
                            &args->clusterCentroids[k * args->N],
                            args->N);
            if (d < minDist[m]) {
                minDist[m] = d;
                args->clusterAssignments[m] = k;
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 4.1 Follow one worker's assignment search
docs.text:
Each worker's args->M is its chunk size: 31,250 points with 32 workers. Worker t processes point indices [t * 31250, (t + 1) * 31250). The pointer still addresses the complete data array, so m is a global point index.

Each point occupies N consecutive doubles: &data[m * N] and &clusterCentroids[k * N] locate point m and centroid k. dist computes their Euclidean distance.

The inner loop scans all K centroids, retaining the shortest distance in minDist[m] and its centroid index in clusterAssignments[m].

All workers read the same data and centroids, which stay fixed during assignment. Each worker writes only its own range of minDist and clusterAssignments, so these writes need no locks. Equal-sized chunks require the point count to be divisible by 32.

docs.title: 4.2 Start the workers and wait for completion
docs.text:
void computeAssignments(WorkerArgs *const workerArgs) {
    static constexpr int MAX_THREADS = 32;
    double *minDist = new double[workerArgs->M];

    for (int m=0; m<workerArgs->M; m++) {
        minDist[m] = 1e30;
        workerArgs->clusterAssignments[m] = -1;
    }

    std::thread workers[MAX_THREADS];
    WorkerArgs args[MAX_THREADS];

    for (int i=0; i<MAX_THREADS; i++) {
        args[i].data = workerArgs->data;
        args[i].clusterCentroids = workerArgs->clusterCentroids;
        args[i].clusterAssignments = workerArgs->clusterAssignments;
        args[i].M = workerArgs->M / MAX_THREADS;
        args[i].K = workerArgs->K;
        args[i].N = workerArgs->N;
        args[i].start = workerArgs->start;
        args[i].end = workerArgs->end;
        args[i].threadId = i;
    }

    for (int i=1; i<MAX_THREADS; i++) {
        workers[i] = std::thread(workerThreadStart, &args[i], minDist);
    }

    workerThreadStart(&args[0], minDist);

    for (int i=1; i<MAX_THREADS; i++) {
        workers[i].join();
    }

    delete[] minDist;
}

workerArgs->M is the total point count; args[i].M is the per-worker chunk size. Distances and assignments are reset each iteration because the centroids have moved.

The caller launches workers 1–31, then runs worker 0. All workers must finish before minDist is freed and the centroid update reads their assignments:

Initialize minDist and assignments
                  |
     +------------+-------------+
     v            v             v
 worker 0     worker 1  ...  worker 31
 own points   own points     own points
     |            |             |
     +------------+-------------+
                  | all workers finish
                  v
          Update centroids
                  |
             Compute cost
                  |
          Test convergence
            /          \
          Done      Next iteration

The measured speedup includes the change from centroid-first to point-first loop order as well as threading.

docs.title: 4.3 Verify and measure
docs.text:
Version Median time (3 runs) Original serial 5813.935 ms Parallel version 2544.944 ms

Overall speedup is 2.28×. Final assignments and centroids match the serial result exactly.

Assignment time drops from 3751.303 ms to 406.651 ms (9.22×). Centroid update and cost calculation remain serial and take about two seconds, limiting the overall speedup.

Complete-run measurements

docs.title: Assignment 2 · Task system
docs.text:
CS149 · Completed

The implementation develops from one shared launch into a scheduler for a graph of launches. Workers claim work under a mutex, run the callback without it, and return to update completion state.

A task is one callback; a launch contains the tasks submitted by one run() or runAsyncWithDeps() call. TaskID identifies the launch. Member names end in _; calls use (). The overview separates the caller, shared state, and workers:

 +----------------------+           +----------------------------------------+
 | Caller               |           | Shared state                           |
 | runAsyncWithDeps()   |-----+     |                                        |
 | run()                |     +---->| waiting_map_ ----> waiting_            |
 | sync()               |     |     |                        |               |
 |                      |     |     |               prev_.empty()            |
 | done_.wait(lk)       |     |     |                        v               |
 +-------------+--------+     +---->| ready_map_   ----> ready_              |
               |                    +----------------------------------------+
               |                                               |
               |                                               v
               |                                 +--------------------------+
               |                                 | worker_                  |
               |                                 | thread_fn()              |
               |                                 +--------------------------+
               |                                               | lk.unlock()
               |                                               v
               |                                 +--------------------------+
               |                                 | runnable->runTask(...)   |
               |                                 +--------------------------+
               |                                               | lk.lock()
               |                                               v
               |                      +--------------------------------------+
               |                      | num_workers_--                       |
               +----------------------| prev_.erase(...)                     |
                 done_.notify_one()   | ready_.splice(...)                   |
                                      | ready_.erase(...)                    |
                                      +--------------------------------------+

Submission takes the lower entry into ready_ when no unfinished dependency remains; otherwise it takes the upper entry into waiting_. A callback return decrements num_workers_. The dependency updates and node removal shown below it require num_left_tasks_ == 0 && num_workers_ == 0; they happen once per completed launch. Workers notify done_ when both lists are empty. The Part A and Part B diagrams expand this overview; their captions identify omitted guards.

Part A keeps runnable_, num_total_tasks_, num_left_tasks_, and num_workers_ on the task-system object. Part B moves these four fields into each TaskNode and adds dependency edges. The constructor starts the sleeping workers; the caller submits nodes; workers advance the graph as launches finish.

Part Contents Part A · Thread pools Shared counters, three worker lifetimes, and caller/worker handoff Part B · Task graphs Node submission, worker execution, and a graph traced through the lists

Appendix · Measurements and checks · Handout

docs.title: Environment and timing
docs.text:
Local measurements use Ubuntu 24.04, an Intel Core i9-13900H (14 physical cores, 20 logical CPUs), eight worker threads, and default CPU scheduling. Both builds use the provided Makefile's -O3 -std=c++11 flags.

The reference Linux x86-64 executable records GCC 9.3.0-17ubuntu1~20.04 in its ELF .comment section. The comparison rebuilds the student code with that same compiler package and with the system's GCC 13.3.0. Both use the host's shared runtime libraries; this is a compiler comparison on the local machine.

Each reported measurement is the minimum of three independent program runs, each invoked with -i 1. This uses fewer repetitions than the normal harness, which takes the minimum of five runs, each with three internal timing iterations. Correctness checks run on every invocation.

The supplied tests time their launches and synchronization. Pool construction and destruction happen outside that region; always-spawn creates its workers inside run(), so those launches include thread creation and joining.

The tables use student time / reference time: smaller is faster. The local performance thresholds are < 1.2 for Part A and < 1.5 for Part B. Part B grades only the sleeping pool, including its synchronous run() interface.

The course grades on an AWS c7g.4xlarge ARM machine. These measurements establish local behavior and do not predict that machine's grade.

Across Part B's 22 measurements, student time is lower in every case. The median time reduction is 24.0%, with reductions ranging from 9.6% to 33.0%. Part A is close to the reference: the median ratios for spawn, spin, and sleep are 1.015, 1.016, and 1.004, respectively.

docs.title: What changes with the compiler?
docs.text:
Times below are milliseconds for the same Part B source and eight-worker setup:

Workload Serial, GCC 9.3 Serial, GCC 13.3 Sleep, GCC 9.3 Sleep, GCC 13.3 Recursive Fibonacci 925.630 587.485 168.355 105.484 Math loop 364.253 345.025 93.043 94.005 Spin between calls 335.818 207.626 172.251 104.566

spin_between_run_calls launches two fib(40) tasks between two light launches. Its useful work changes substantially with compiler-generated Fibonacci code. Switching from GCC 9.3 to GCC 13.3 improves serial time by 1.62× and sleeping-pool time by 1.65×. The pool's speedup over its own serial build stays close to two: 1.95× with GCC 9.3 and 1.99× with GCC 13.3.

The corrected reference sleeping-pool time is 214.807 ms. Comparing GCC 13 to this GCC 9 reference gives a ratio of 0.487; using GCC 9 for both gives 0.802. A large part of that apparent advantage comes from the compiler, while the older build still passes comfortably. The math-loop times change much less.

Complete samples and source hashes · Compiler package versions and hashes

docs.title: Reference timer correction
docs.text:
The current source uses std::chrono::steady_clock. The supplied Linux x86-64 reference binary instead converts TSC ticks using a sampled CPU MHz value. On this machine that conversion can disagree with the constant-rate TSC.

tests/reference_timer.py measures seconds per TSC tick against CLOCK_MONOTONIC, using the median of five 100 ms samples. It reads the conversion factor from its own reference child process and applies:

corrected reference milliseconds
    = reported milliseconds
    × measured seconds per TSC tick / reference seconds per TSC tick

The binary and its workload remain unchanged. The correction applies to its reported times; process startup and shutdown are not substituted for the timed region. The saved results include each correction factor.

docs.title: Correctness checks
docs.text:
The supplied simple_test_sync, simple_test_async, strict_diamond_deps_async, and strict_graph_deps_large_async passed with one and eight workers in the current GCC 13 build.

The standalone additional check exercises the sleeping pool with one, two, and eight workers:

  • 300 short A → B chains per worker count. A delays briefly so B is likely to be submitted before A finishes.
  • 50 graphs of 48 launches per worker count, with 1–7 tasks per launch. Each graph includes a chain and additional randomly selected predecessor edges.
  • Every task ID must execute exactly once, each successor checks its predecessors' completed counts, and sync() must return with every task finished.
  • Repeated sync() calls and 30 idle pool construction/destruction cycles.

All checks passed with libstdc++ debug iterators under both GCC 9.3 and GCC 13.3. They exercise the queue transitions and repeated use of the worker pool.

From the repository root:

g++ -O1 -g -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG -std=c++11 -pthread \
    -Iasst2/part_b docs/assets/benchmarks/a2_checks.cpp \
    asst2/part_b/tasksys.cpp -o /tmp/a2-checks
timeout 30s /tmp/a2-checks

docs.title: Reproduce the performance measurements
docs.text:
The measurement script builds in temporary copies. Supply a working GCC 9.3.0 compiler and choose a new output directory:

python3 docs/assets/benchmarks/benchmark_a2.py . /tmp/a2-measurements \
    --cxx9 /path/to/g++-9 -n 8 --rounds 3 --iterations 1

Use --rounds 5 --iterations 3 for the normal harness's repetition counts. The script records source hashes, compiler versions, raw timings, and corrected reference timings. An extracted compiler may also need its library directory in LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

For the usual grading report, build the selected part and run the harness from that directory:

cd asst2/part_b
make
python3 ../tests/run_test_harness.py -n 8 -a

For Part A, run the same commands from asst2/part_a and omit -a.

docs.title: Part A · One shared launch
docs.text: All three implementations use the same work-distribution idea: publish one runnable_ and let workers claim task IDs from a shared counter. Each worker can execute several tasks; num_threads_ bounds the workers created.

docs.title: Members
docs.text:
Each class derives directly from ITaskSystem; the additions below compare their designs. TaskSystemSerial adds no data members and executes a local loop.

TaskSystemParallelSpawn introduces the shared launch state:

Member Role and changes num_threads_ Constructor argument; fixed worker count. runnable_ nullptr → caller's pointer → nullptr after completion. num_total_tasks_ Initially 0; set by run(), fixed during that launch. num_left_tasks_ Initially 0; set to the launch size, decremented on claim. num_workers_ Initially 0; incremented on claim, decremented after the callback. mutex_ Shared mutex, allocated at construction and deleted at destruction.

The pool versions retain those members and add:

Class Added members Purpose TaskSystemParallelThreadPoolSpinning worker_, flag_ Persistent worker array; atomic flag_ stays true until shutdown. TaskSystemParallelThreadPoolSleeping undone_, done_ Workers wait on undone_; the caller waits on done_.

Part A stores the mutex and condition variables through pointers. The caller owns the runnable and keeps it alive until run() returns.

num_left_tasks, num_total_tasks, and lk are local variables from the source.

docs.title: 1. Claim, compute, account
docs.text:
thread_fn()
                               |
                               v
          +------------------------------------------+
          | num_left_tasks = num_left_tasks_         |
     +--->| num_total_tasks = num_total_tasks_       |
     |    | num_left_tasks_--                        |
     |    | num_workers_++                           |
     |    +------------------------------------------+
     |                         | mutex_->unlock()
     |                         v
     |    +------------------------------------------+
     |    | runnable_->runTask(num_left_tasks - 1,   |
     |    |                    num_total_tasks)      |
     |    +------------------------------------------+
     |                         | mutex_->lock()
     |                         v
     |    +------------------------------------------+
     |    | num_workers_--                           |
     |    +------------------------------------------+
     |                         |
     +-------------------------+
            num_left_tasks_ > 0

The diagram starts with *mutex_ held and runnable_ && num_left_tasks_ != 0. Pool workers also check !flag_ at the start of their outer loop and exit if it is true. Idle behavior differs between the three versions, as shown below. Exact entry and loop guards are in each class's thread_fn() in asst2/part_a/tasksys.cpp.

num_left_tasks_ counts unclaimed tasks. num_workers_ counts workers executing a claimed task. A worker saves the old task count, decrements it, and calls runTask(num_left_tasks - 1, num_total_tasks), so IDs are assigned from N - 1 down to 0.

Only claiming and accounting hold the mutex. The callback runs outside it. run() recognizes completion when both counters are zero; all IDs may have been claimed while workers are still computing.

Spawn releases the mutex between worker-loop iterations. The spinning and sleeping pools can keep it from accounting through the next claim.

For a three-task launch P, one possible two-worker execution is:

 Event                         num_total_tasks_  num_left_tasks_  num_workers_
 constructed                           0                0              0
 run(P, 3): runnable_ = P               3                3              0
 claim task 2                          3                2              1
 claim task 1                          3                1              2
 finish task 2                         3                1              1
 claim task 0                          3                0              2
 finish task 1                         3                0              1
 finish task 0                         3                0              0
 run(): runnable_ = nullptr            3                0              0

num_total_tasks_ retains the completed launch's size until the next run(). The pointer is cleared only after both live counters reach zero. Spawn and spin start each subsequent launch with the previous completion's zero active count; the sleeping version also explicitly assigns num_workers_ = 0 when publishing.

docs.title: 2. Change the worker lifetime
docs.text:
This timeline labels thread actions across two calls:

               ctor        run #1             gap       run #2          dtor
               ----        ------             ---       ------          ----
 Always spawn  (none)      [create/work/join]  (none)    [create/work/join]  -

 Spinning      [create] --> [work] ----------> [spin] --> [work] ------> [stop/join]

 Sleeping      [create] --> [work] ----------> [wait] --> [work] ------> [wake/join]
               |                                                          |
               +---------------- same pool workers -----------------------+

Spawn's local worker array is created, joined, and deleted inside run(). Both pools start worker_ in the constructor and join it in the destructor. flag_ changes from true to false under the mutex at shutdown; sleep also notifies undone_ before joining. Shared storage is deleted after the joins.

docs.title: 3. Hand a launch to the sleeping pool
docs.text:
run()                                                 thread_fn()
   |                                                     |
   | runnable_ = P                                       |
   | num_total_tasks_ = N                                |
   | num_left_tasks_ = N                                 |
   | num_workers_ = 0                                    |
   | lk.unlock()                                         |
   +-------------- undone_->notify_all() ---------------->
   |                                                     | lk.lock()
   | lk.lock()                                           | num_left_tasks_--
   |                                                     | num_workers_++
   | done_->wait(lk)                                     | lk.unlock()
   |                                                     | runnable_->runTask(...)
   |                                                     | lk.lock()
   |                                                     | num_workers_--
   |                                                     |
   <-------------- done_->notify_one() ------------------+
   |                                                     |
   |                                                     |
   | num_left_tasks_ == 0 && num_workers_ == 0           |
   | runnable_ = nullptr                                 | undone_->wait(lk)
   | lk.unlock()                                         |
   |                                                     |
   v                                                     v

The diagram follows a call that waits for completion. P is the runnable pointer and N the launch size. The omitted wait conditions are:

  • Before claiming, a worker waits on undone_ if !runnable_ || num_left_tasks_ == 0.
  • After a callback, if num_left_tasks_ == 0, the worker leaves its task loop when num_workers_ == 0; otherwise it waits on undone_.
  • The caller clears runnable_ when both counters are zero; otherwise it waits on done_. It checks again after waking, so a call may also finish without taking the illustrated wait path.

These checks hold *mutex_; wait(lk) releases it while sleeping and reacquires it before returning. Workers notify done_ after leaving their task loop and remain alive for later calls. The full branches are in the sleeping pool's thread_fn() and run() in asst2/part_a/tasksys.cpp.

Part B · Multiple launches and dependencies

docs.title: Part B · A graph of launches
docs.text: The single shared launch from Part A becomes a TaskNode. Each node stores its runnable_, task counters, unfinished predecessors (prev_), and successors (next_). The system's taskID_ counter assigns each launch its ID.

docs.title: Members
docs.text:
Part A stores the launch fields on the pool; Part B moves them into each node:

 runnable_          -----+       ready_ / waiting_
 num_total_tasks_   -----+              |
 num_left_tasks_    -----+-----> TaskNode
 num_workers_       -----+       |-- runnable_
                                |-- num_total_tasks_
                                |-- num_left_tasks_
                                |-- num_workers_
                                |-- taskID_
                                |-- prev_
                                +-- next_

Each node starts with the caller's pointer, its total task count, the same count of unclaimed tasks, and zero active workers. The pointer and total remain fixed; claims and callback returns change the two live counters as in Part A. The node also adds:

Field Role and changes taskID_ This launch's assigned ID; fixed until removal. prev_ Unfinished predecessor IDs; completion removes them until empty. next_ Initially empty; later dependent submissions append their IDs. Completion walks these edges.

The pool's members are:

Members Role and changes num_threads_, worker_, flag_ Fixed worker count and persistent array; atomic flag_ changes from true to false at shutdown. taskID_ Next unused launch ID, starting at 0; each accepted launch increments it. sync() does not reset it. waiting_, waiting_map_ Initially empty; nodes with unfinished predecessors and their ID → iterator index; nodes leave when unblocked. ready_, ready_map_ Initially empty; dependency-ready nodes and their index; nodes stay until all their callbacks finish. mutex_ Protects ID allocation, lists, maps, dependency edges, and counters. undone_, done_ Workers wait on undone_; the caller waits on done_.

Unlike Part A, the mutex and condition variables are value members. They are constructed before workers start and destroyed after the destructor joins them. The system's taskID_ advances; each node's taskID_ is a fixed copy.

taskID, deps_fn, ready_node, next_node, prev_node, and lk are local variables from the source.

docs.title: 1. Submit and connect a node
docs.text:
runAsyncWithDeps()
                                 |
                   +---------------------------+
                   | mutex_.lock()             |
                   | taskID = taskID_++        |
                   | deps_fn = deps            |
                   +---------------------------+
                                 |
             +---------------------------------------+
             | waiting_map_.find(deps[i])            |
             | ready_map_.find(deps[i])              |
             | deps_fn.erase(...)                    |
             +---------------------------------------+
                                 |
                         deps_fn.empty()
                     true /           \ false
                         v               v
   +-----------------------------+   +--------------------------------------+
   | ready_.push_back(...)       |   | prev_node->next_.push_back(taskID)   |
   | ready_map_[taskID] = ...    |   | waiting_.push_back(...)              |
   | prev_ = []                  |   | waiting_map_[taskID] = ...           |
   +-----------------------------+   | prev_ = deps_fn                      |
                  |                  +--------------------------------------+
                  |                                      |
                  +-------------------+------------------+
                                      v
                        +----------------------------+
                        | mutex_.unlock()            |
                        | undone_.notify_all()       |
                        | return taskID              |
                        +----------------------------+

The diagram starts after the input guard: a null runnable or zero tasks returns -1 before allocating an ID. Empty deps skips the lookup box and enters ready_ directly. Otherwise the box repeats for each dependency, and deps_fn.erase(...) runs only when that valid ID is absent from both maps, meaning its launch has completed. These checks and edge updates hold mutex_. Exact branches are in runAsyncWithDeps() in asst2/part_b/tasksys.cpp.

The maps store iterators to nodes in their corresponding lists. Workers may start execution while the caller submits later nodes.

docs.title: 2. Execute and advance the graph
docs.text:
thread_fn()
                                  |
                                  v
             +----------------------------------------+<--------------------+
             | ready_                                 |                     |
             | num_left_tasks_ > 0                    |                     |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
                                  |                                         |
                          true    |    false --> undone_.wait(lk) ----------+
                                  v                                         |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
             | num_left_tasks_--                      |                     |
             | num_workers_++                         |                     |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
                                  | lk.unlock()                             |
                                  v                                         |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
             | runnable->runTask(...)                 |                     |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
                                  | lk.lock()                               |
                                  v                                         |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
             | num_workers_--                         |                     |
             | num_left_tasks_ == 0 &&                |                     |
             | num_workers_ == 0                      |                     |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
                          true    |    false -------------------------------+
                                  v                                         |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
             | next_node->prev_.erase(...)            |                     |
             | if (next_node->prev_.empty())          |                     |
             |   ready_.splice(...)                   |                     |
             |   ready_map_[taskID] = ...             |                     |
             |   waiting_map_.erase(taskID)           |                     |
             |   undone_.notify_all()                 |                     |
             | ready_map_.erase(...)                  |                     |
             | ready_.erase(...) / ready_.pop_front() |                     |
             +----------------------------------------+                     |
                                  |                                         |
               ready_.empty() && waiting_.empty() -- false -----------------+
                                  | true
                                  v
                             lk.unlock()
                           done_.notify_one()

The diagram shows the inner loop, entered only when !ready_.empty(). The outer loop first exits on !flag_ and waits on undone_ when ready_.empty() && waiting_.empty(). After waking, it rechecks emptiness before entering the inner loop. Unqualified counters belong to the selected node; next_node is a successor iterator. The worker copies the selected pointer and counts into locals before unlocking for the callback. All queue, edge, and counter updates hold mutex_.

Workers scan ready_ past nodes with no unclaimed tasks. A node with num_left_tasks_ == 0 may still have active workers, so it remains in the list. If no task is available, the worker waits on undone_ and selects again after waking.

Completion visits each successor in next_. The successor moves to ready_ only after its prev_ becomes empty. splice transfers the same node and preserves its iterator for the map update.

The diagram groups two cleanup checks. Non-front removal requires both counters to be zero and ready_node != ready_.begin(). The code then independently checks the front node's two counters before using pop_front. Both paths keep mutex_ held through dependency updates and node removal. See thread_fn() in asst2/part_b/tasksys.cpp for the exact scan, wait, and cleanup branches.

docs.title: 3. Follow one graph through the lists
docs.text:
The letters A, B, C, and D below name launches with IDs 0, 1, 2, and 3. Each listed taskID_ is also a key in the corresponding map. The pool has two workers, and submission advances the system's taskID_ from 0 to 4.

                         +---- B ----+
                         |           |
                  A -----+           +---- D
                         |           |
                         +---- C ----+

 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
 | Event          | ready_ + ready_map_                | waiting_ + waiting_map_            |
 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
 | Submitted      | taskID_=0; prev_=[]                | taskID_=1; prev_=[0]               |
 |                | next_=[1,2]                        | next_=[3]                          |
 |                | num_left_tasks_=2; num_workers_=0  | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |
 |                |                                    | taskID_=2; prev_=[0]               |
 |                |                                    | next_=[3]                          |
 |                |                                    | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |
 |                |                                    | taskID_=3; prev_=[1,2]             |
 |                |                                    | next_=[]                           |
 |                |                                    | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |
 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
 | 0 finishes     | taskID_=1; prev_=[]                | taskID_=3; prev_=[1,2]             |
 |                | next_=[3]                          | next_=[]                           |
 |                | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |
 |                | taskID_=2; prev_=[]                |                                    |
 |                | next_=[3]                          |                                    |
 |                | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |                                    |
 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
 | 1 finishes     | taskID_=2; prev_=[]                | taskID_=3; prev_=[2]               |
 | 2 computing    | next_=[3]                          | next_=[]                           |
 |                | num_left_tasks_=0; num_workers_=1  | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |
 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
 | 2 finishes     | taskID_=3; prev_=[]                | []                                 |
 |                | next_=[]                           |                                    |
 |                | num_left_tasks_=1; num_workers_=0  |                                    |
 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
 | 3 finishes     | []                                 | []                                 |
 +----------------+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+

All four launches are submitted before a worker claims a task. A has two tasks; B, C, and D have one each. B and C can run concurrently after A finishes. If B finishes first, D still waits for C. C stays in ready_ with num_left_tasks_ = 0 and num_workers_ = 1. Their completion order may reverse.

Node removal destroys that launch record and its vectors. It does not delete the caller's runnable. Removing the ID from its map lets later submissions recognize it as completed.

docs.title: 4. Return to the caller
docs.text:
The three entry points share the sleeping workers, with these distinct paths:

Entry point Queue operation Return condition run() Append a dependency-free node to ready_ and ready_map_; notify undone_ ready_.empty() runAsyncWithDeps() Follow the submission diagram Node published and ID returned sync() Add no node; wait on done_ ready_.empty() && waiting_.empty()

The handout uses one calling thread and separates synchronous and asynchronous launches. In synchronous mode waiting_ stays empty, so run() checks only ready_.

The worker notifies done_ after it observes both lists empty. The caller rechecks its condition under mutex_. Completed launches have already been removed, so this also accounts for the end of their callbacks.

After this example's sync(), all four containers are empty, the system's taskID_ remains 4, and flag_ remains true. The workers stay alive.

Shutdown sets flag_ = false under the mutex, notifies undone_, joins every worker, and deletes worker_.
